We see that vectors $( L u_{1}, \dots, L u_{n} )$ are orthogonal but not orthonormal. Moreover, the length of $L u_{i}$ is $\sqrt{\lambda_{i}}.$ Normalizing gives the orthonormal and linearly independent ordered set

$$
\left(\frac {L u _ {1}}{\sqrt {\lambda_ {1}}}, \dots , \frac {L u _ {n}}{\sqrt {\lambda_ {n}}}\right).
$$

In general, this cannot be a basis for $W$ since $\ker L=\{0\}$ $\dim L(V)=$ $\dim V$ , and in turn $\dim V\leq\dim W$ , so n $\leq m.$

However, it is a subset of the eigenvectors of $L L^{*}$ so there is an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of $L L^{*}$ of the form

$$
O ^ {\prime} = \left(\frac {L u _ {1}}{\sqrt {\lambda_ {1}}}, \dots , \frac {L u _ {n}}{\sqrt {\lambda_ {n}}}, v _ {n + 1}, \dots , v _ {m}\right) =: \left(v _ {1}, \dots , v _ {m}\right).
$$

Now lets compute the matrix of $L$ with respect to the orthonormal basis $O=(u_{1},\dots,u_{n})$ for $V$ and the orthonormal basis $O^{\prime}=(v_{1},\dots,v_{m})$ for $W.$

As usual, our starting point is the computation of L acting on the input basis vectors;

$$
\begin{array}{l} L O = \left(L u _ {1}, \dots , L u _ {n}\right) = \left(\sqrt {\lambda_ {1}} v _ {1}, \dots , \sqrt {\lambda_ {n}} v _ {n}\right) \\ = \left(v _ {1}, \dots , v _ {m}\right) \left( \begin{array}{c c c c} \sqrt {\lambda_ {1}} & 0 & \dots & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt {\lambda_ {2}} & \dots & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & \dots & \sqrt {\lambda_ {n}} \\ 0 & 0 & \dots & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & \dots & 0 \end{array} \right). \\ \end{array}
$$

The result is very close to diagonalization; the numbers $\sqrt{\lambda_{i}}$ along the leading diagonal are called the singular values of L.

Example 155 Let the matrix of a linear transformation be

$$
M = \left( \begin{array}{c c} \frac {1}{2} & \frac {1}{2} \\ - 1 & 1 \\ - \frac {1}{2} & - \frac {1}{2} \end{array} \right).
$$

ker $M=\{0\}$ while

$$
M ^ {T} M = \left( \begin{array}{c c} \frac {3}{2} & - \frac {1}{2} \\ - \frac {1}{2} & \frac {3}{2} \end{array} \right)
$$

which has eigenvalues and eigenvectors

which has eigenvalues and eigenvectors

$$
\lambda = 1, u _ {1} := \left( \begin{array}{c} \frac {1}{\sqrt {2}} \\ \frac {1}{\sqrt {2}} \end{array} \right); \quad \lambda = 2, u _ {2} := \left( \begin{array}{c} \frac {1}{\sqrt {2}} \\ - \frac {1}{\sqrt {2}} \end{array} \right).
$$

so our orthonormal input basis is

$$
O = \left(\binom {\frac {1}{\sqrt {2}}} {\frac {1}{\sqrt {2}}}, \binom {\frac {1}{\sqrt {2}}}{- \frac {1}{\sqrt {2}}}\right).
$$

These are called the right singular vectors of M. The vectors

$$
M u _ {1} = \left( \begin{array}{c} \frac {1}{\sqrt {2}} \\ 0 \\ - \frac {1}{\sqrt {2}} \end{array} \right) \mathrm {a n d} M u _ {2} = \left( \begin{array}{c} 0 \\ - \sqrt {2} \\ 0 \end{array} \right)
$$

are eigenvectors of

$$
M M ^ {T} = \left( \begin{array}{c c c} \frac {1}{2} & 0 & - \frac {1}{2} \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ - \frac {1}{2} & 0 & \frac {1}{2} \end{array} \right)
$$

with eigenvalues 1 and 2, respectively. The third eigenvector (with eigenvalue 0) of $MM^{T}$ is

$$
v _ {3} = \left( \begin{array}{c c} \frac {1}{\sqrt {2}} \\ 0 \\ \frac {1}{\sqrt {2}} \end{array} \right).
$$

The eigenvectors $M u_{1}$ and $M u_{2}$ are necessarily orthogonal, dividing them by their lengths we obtain the left singular vectors and in turn our orthonormal output basis

$$
O ^ {\prime} = \left(\left( \begin{array}{c} \frac {1}{\sqrt {2}} \\ 0 \\ - \frac {1}{\sqrt {2}} \end{array} \right), \left( \begin{array}{c} 0 \\ - 1 \\ 0 \end{array} \right), \left( \begin{array}{c} \frac {1}{\sqrt {2}} \\ 0 \\ \frac {1}{\sqrt {2}} \end{array} \right)\right).
$$

The new matrix $M^{\prime}$ of the linear transformation given by M with respect to the bases O and $O^{\prime}$ is

$$
M ^ {\prime} = \left( \begin{array}{c c} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt {2} \\ 0 & 0 \end{array} \right),
$$

the singular values are 1, $\sqrt{2}.$

Finally note that arranging the column vectors of O and $O^{\prime}$ into change of basis matrices

the singular values are 1, $\sqrt{2}.$

Finally note that arranging the column vectors of O and $O^{\prime}$ into change of basis matrices

$$
P = \left( \begin{array}{c c} \frac {1}{\sqrt {2}} & \frac {1}{\sqrt {2}} \\ \frac {1}{\sqrt {2}} & - \frac {1}{\sqrt {2}} \end{array} \right), \quad Q = \left( \begin{array}{c c c} \frac {1}{\sqrt {2}} & 0 & \frac {1}{\sqrt {2}} \\ 0 & - 1 & 0 \\ - \frac {1}{\sqrt {2}} & 0 & \frac {1}{\sqrt {2}} \end{array} \right),
$$

we have, as usual,

$$
M ^ {\prime} = Q ^ {- 1} M P.
$$

Singular vectors and values have a very nice geometric interpretation; they provide an orthonormal bases for the domain and range of L and give the factors by which L stretches the orthonormal input basis vectors. This is depicted below for the example we just computed.

Definition A field $\mathbb{F}$ is a set with two operations + and $\cdot$ , such that for all a,b,c $\in\mathbb{F}$ the following axioms are satisfied:

A1. Addition is associative $( a+b)+c=a+( b+c).$

A2. There exists an additive identity 0.

A3. Addition is commutative $a+b=b+a.$

A4. There exists an additive inverse $-a$.

M1. Multiplication is associative $(a \cdot b) \cdot c = a \cdot (b \cdot c)$.

M2. There exists a multiplicative identity 1.

M3. Multiplication is commutative $a \cdot b=b\cdot a.$

M4. There exists a multiplicative inverse $a^{-1}$ if $a\neq0.$

D. The distributive law holds $a \cdot(b+c)=ab+ac.$

Roughly, all of the above mean that you have notions of +,-, $\times$ and $\div$ just as for regular real numbers.

Fields are a very beautiful structure; some examples are rational numbers $\mathbb{Q}$ , real numbers $\mathbb{R}$ , and complex numbers $\mathbb{C}$ . These examples are infinite, however this does not necessarily have to be the case. The smallest

example of a field has just two elements, $\mathbb{Z}_{2}=\{0,1\}$ or bits. The rules for addition and multiplication are the usual ones save that

$$
1 + 1 = 0.
$$

Now, integration is a linear transformation from the space $V$ of all integrable functions (don't be confused between the definition of a linear function above, and integrable functions $f(x)$ which here are the vectors in $V$ ) to the real numbers $\mathbb{R}$ , because $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}(\alpha f(x)+\beta g(x))dx=\alpha \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)dx+\beta\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}g(x)dx.$

But $(-1)\cdot u+u=(-1)\cdot u+1\cdot u=(-1+1)\cdot u=0. u=0$ (at each step in this chain of equalities we have used the fact that V is a vector space and therefore can use its vector space rules). But since $\left( \begin{array}{c} x \\ y \\ 0 \end{array} \right) + \left( \begin{array}{c} z \\ w \\ 0 \end{array} \right) = \left( \begin{array}{c} x + z \\ y + w \\ 0 \end{array} \right)$ so is their sum (because vectors in U are those whose third component vanishes).
